=== Findings of Fact Conclusions of Law and Proposed Order for Mark Allan Bradbury.docx ===
SOAH DOCKET NUMBER 473-26-16349 PUC DOCKET NUMBER 59475

I, Mark Allan Bradbury (“Pro-Se Intervenor # 634”) respectfully submit these Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law regarding the routing of the proposed 765 kV transmission line affecting Concho, and McCulloch Counties, Texas on behalf of myself and Heart of Texas Bowhunting, LLC.

PART I
PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT
Jurisdiction and Need
Applicants seek CCN authority to construct the Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV transmission project.
The proposed transmission line would traverse portions of Bell, Burnet, Lampasas, McCulloch, Menard, Concho, Schleicher, Sutton, Crockett, Reagan, Irion, Tom Green, and surrounding counties.
The proposed facility consists of extra-high-voltage transmission infrastructure including lattice and/or monopole structures, conductors, access roads, construction staging areas, and associated facilities.
The project would require a permanent transmission easement corridor generally ranging from approximately 200 to 350 feet in width.
Construction would require substantial temporary disturbance beyond the permanent easement for access roads, structure assembly areas, conductor pulling sites, material laydown yards, and construction staging areas.
Jared Gurley further confirmed that the Project's purpose is associated with the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. Hearing Vol. 3 at 146–147.
Jared Gurley also acknowledged that Concho and McCulloch Counties are already energized and supported by the existing electric grid. Hearing Vol. 3 at 146–147.
Commission Staff witness John Poole testified that the project is intended to move power from West Texas generation resources to load centers elsewhere in ERCOT. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 194–195.
Mr. Poole testified that the need for the project is not related to transmission needs within the counties crossed by the route. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 194–195.
Mr. Poole testified that no substations are located between Bell County East and Big Hill East that would receive service from the proposed transmission line. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 194–195.
ROUTE SELECTION METHODOLOGY
The Commission is required to consider community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers.
The Commission is further required to consider prudent utilization of existing compatible rights-of-way and corridors.
No route is entirely without impact; therefore, the Commission must determine which route best balances the applicable routing criteria.
Former PUC Commissioner Barry T. Smitherman testified that he did not believe any route crossing the Colorado River is in compliance with PURA or the rules. Dr. Smitherman Cross, June 11th Transcript, at 199.
The arbitrarily chosen study area boundary effectively eliminated routes that would have bypassed the Colorado River and been adjacent to additional existing routes of way. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 140–149.
Applicants evaluated several potential route alternatives before identifying Route 894 as the preferred route.
Applicants testified that route selection was performed through a holistic balancing of routing factors and that no prescribed weighting formula exists under PURA or Commission rules.
Commission Staff witness John Poole testified that his recommendation utilized no mathematical formula, weighting system, or quantitative methodology assigning relative importance to competing routing criteria. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 197.
Mr. Poole testified that his testimony contains no formula explaining how the statutory routing criteria were balanced. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 197.
Mr. Poole testified that community values, historical values, aesthetic values, environmental integrity, engineering considerations, and costs are routing factors that must be considered by the Commission.
Community Values
Community values are a routing criterion under PURA §37.056(c)(4).
Residents of Concho, and McCulloch Counties expressed concerns regarding ranch fragmentation, visual impacts, cultural resources, hunting impacts, and loss of rural character. Bradbury Direct Testimony, et al.
Preservation of rural ranching landscapes constitutes a significant community value within the affected counties. Bradbury Direct Testimony, et al.
Community values and historical values are routing criteria considered by the Commission.
Historic ranching landscapes constitute important community values in Concho, and McCulloch Counties.
Historic Ranching Landscapes
Historical values are a routing criterion under PURA §37.056(c)(4).
Routes 894/894 WM1 bisect the heritage/century Ford Ranch landscape. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 144–145.
Applicant witness Russell Marusak testified Applicants were unaware of the heritage-ranch status of Ford Ranch during route development. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 144–145.
Historical landscapes may be affected by the introduction of major utility infrastructure even where no historic structure is physically removed.
Visual fragmentation and alteration of landscape integrity are relevant considerations under the historical-values criterion.
Cultural Resources
Staff witness Poole identified approximately 100 archaeological sites within 1,000 feet of candidate routes. Poole Direct Testimony at 41.
Staff witness Poole identified approximately 23 cemeteries within 1,000 feet of candidate routes. Poole Direct Testimony at 41.
Applicants' Cultural Resources Attachment 21 identifies recorded archaeological sites associated with route links in Concho and McCulloch Counties.
Recorded archaeological site 41CC331 is associated with Link N12 in Concho County. Applicants’ Cultural Resources Attachment 21, at 6.
Recorded archaeological site 41CC350 is associated with Link N12 in Concho County. Applicants’ Cultural Resources Attachment 21, at 6.
Recorded archaeological site 41MK48 is associated with Link M12 in McCulloch County. Applicants’ Cultural Resources Attachment 21, at 8.
Recorded archaeological site 41MN75 is associated with Link N2 in Menard County. Applicants’ Cultural Resources Attachment 21, at 8.
The occurrence of multiple archaeological sites along adjacent route links, M12, N2 and N12, demonstrates elevated archaeological sensitivity in portions of Concho and McCulloch Counties.
Construction of a 765-kV transmission line requires foundations, access roads, conductor pull sites, staging areas, and maintenance access that may affect cultural resources well beyond the centerline.
Links M12, N2, and N12 occur within a culturally sensitive landscape.
HUNTING, WILDLIFE, AND RURAL LAND USE
The affected ranches are used for livestock production, wildlife management, hunting, and recreational purposes. Bradbury Direct Testimony, et al.
Hunting operations constitute an important land use within Concho and McCulloch, Counties. Bradbury Direct Testimony, et al.
Wildlife management and hunting leases contribute materially to the economic use of affected ranches. Bradbury Direct Testimony, et al.
Mr. Marusak acknowledged that bow-hunting stands would not ordinarily remain within the cleared transmission right-of-way. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 145.
Transmission easements reduce the area available for certain hunting and wildlife-management activities.
Corridor Utilization
Prudent utilization of existing compatible rights-of-way is a statutory routing consideration.
Consolidation of infrastructure reduces fragmentation of previously undisturbed lands.
During cross-examination, Mr. Marusak acknowledged that Applicants did not evaluate the alternative southern corridor identified by Pro-Se Intervenor Mark Bradbury. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 140–149.
Mr. Marusak acknowledged that existing transmission facilities occur along portions of the corridor identified by Mr. Bradbury. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 142–149.
Mr. Marusak acknowledged that Applicants did not evaluate routing along the southern existing transmission-line corridor extending from Lampasas toward Big Hill East. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 142–149.
Evidence presented during cross-examination suggested substantially greater infrastructure consolidation could occur within portions of that corridor. Mr. Bradbury Direct Testimony, Exhibit 003.









Table of Routes – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables


Route 392 – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables
Route 392 creates substantially greater residential impacts than Routes 410, 487 894 and 894 WM1.
Route 392 creates substantially greater cultural-resource impacts than Routes 487, 894 and 894 WM1.
Route 392 is longer than Route 487.
Route 410 – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables
Route 410 ranks below other routes in comparable ROW/property-boundary paralleling.
Route 410 creates substantially greater cultural-resource impacts than Route 487.
Route 410 is longer than Route 487.
The record establishes that Route 410 provides poor performance across most of the statutory routing criteria.
Route 487 – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables
Route 487 ranks third among evaluated routes for percentage of compatible ROW utilization.
Route 487 utilizes significantly more ROW than Routes 894/894 WM1.
Route 487 has less potential to impact archeological/historic sites.
Commission Staff witness John Poole testified that Route 487 has the most advantages and is superior to the other proposed alternative routes. Poole Direct Testimony, at 65.
Route 894 – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables
Route 894 is Applicant’s preferred route.
Route 894 ranks forty-seventh among evaluated routes for percentage of compatible ROW utilization.
Route 894 crosses two recorded cultural-resource sites, within a culturally sensitive corridor on links M12, N2, and N12.
Route 894 utilizes substantially less compatible ROW than Route 487.
Route 894 utilizes substantially less existing transmission infrastructure than Route 487.
Route 894 is longer than Route 487.
Route 894 Western Mod 1 – Applicants 59475 Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data tables
Route 894 WM1 was developed by Link R1 Opposition Landowners specifically to avoid their properties. Hearing Tr. Vol. 3 at 45.
Link R1 Opposition Landowners argue that windfarms along Route 894 WM1 provide proof of an existing industrial corridor.  Initial Brief of Link R1 Opposition Landowners at 11.
In fact, almost all of the windfarms in McCulloch and Concho Counties are over 8 miles North of the proposed Route 894 WM1 at Link N12, and most landowners along Link N12 are actively against windfarms in the area.
Route 894 WM1 ranks worse than Route 894 among evaluated routes for percentage of compatible ROW utilization.
Route 894 WM1 crosses two recorded cultural-resource sites, within a culturally sensitive corridor on links M12, N2, and N12 with 19 recorded cultural resources within 1000 feet of route centerline.
Route 894 WM1 has a larger ecological impact than Route 487.
Route 894 WM1 utilizes substantially less compatible ROW than Route 487.
Route 894 WM1 utilizes substantially less existing transmission infrastructure than Route 487.
Route 894 WM1 is longer than Route 487.
Ultimate Findings
Route 392 places disproportionate weight on corridor utilization and produces excessive residential and cultural-resource impacts.
Route 410 does not perform as well as other routes on multiple routing factors.
Routes 894 and 894 WM1 would create cumulative impacts including visual intrusion, vegetation clearing, wildlife-habitat disturbance, cultural-resource impacts, hunting impacts, ranch fragmentation, and permanent easement burdens.
Routes 894 and 894 WM1 underperform Route 487 in utilization of compatible right-of-way.
Routes 894 and 894 WM1 underperform Route 487 in utilization of existing transmission infrastructure.
Route 487 provides the best overall balance of community values, historical values, environmental integrity, cultural-resource protection, corridor utilization, infrastructure consolidation, and moderation of impacts on affected landowners.


PART II
PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
JURISDICTION
The Commission has jurisdiction pursuant to PURA Chapter 37.
PURA §37.056(c)(4) requires consideration of community values, recreational and park areas, historical values, aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and cost.
16 TAC §25.101 requires the Commission to route transmission lines so as to reasonably moderate impacts on affected landowners and communities.
The Administrative Law Judges have authority to issue a Proposal for Decision pursuant to PURA, the Administrative Procedure Act, and the Commission's procedural rules.
APPLICABLE ROUTING STANDARD
PURA §37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider:
community values;
recreational and park areas;
historical values;
aesthetic values;
environmental integrity; and
probable improvement of service and lowering of cost to consumers.
The Commission is not required to select Applicants' preferred route and may select any route supported by substantial evidence.
The Commission is not required to select the route with the fewest habitable structures, the shortest route, or the lowest cost route if another route better satisfies the overall statutory routing criteria.
The Commission's routing decision requires balancing all statutory routing factors rather than elevating any single factor above all others.
The Commission may consider historic ranching landscapes as part of community values and historical values.
The Commission may consider archaeological resources and cultural-resource landscapes when evaluating route alternatives.
The Commission may assign substantial weight to prudent utilization of existing compatible rights-of-way.
The record demonstrates that Applicants did not evaluate at least one major alternative corridor containing substantial existing transmission infrastructure. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 140–149.
COMMUNITY VALUES
Community values include existing land uses, ranching operations, wildlife-management activities, hunting operations, agricultural production, rural residential character, and other characteristics that define the nature of affected communities.
The Commission may properly consider impacts to ranching operations, wildlife-management properties, hunting leases, and agricultural operations under the community-values criterion.
The Commission may consider evidence that Concho and McCulloch Counties bear substantial project impacts despite already being served by the existing transmission system. Findings 6-10.
The Commission may assign weight to evidence demonstrating that larger ranch properties are more susceptible to fragmentation from new utility corridors. Findings 22-30.
HISTORICAL VALUES
Historical values include both individually identified historic resources and broader historic landscapes.
Historic ranching landscapes are properly considered under PURA §37.056(c)(4).
The Commission may consider impacts to the Ford Ranch historic landscape when evaluating competing routes.
Historical landscape preservation is a legitimate factor supporting route selection.
The record demonstrates that Applicants were unaware of the heritage/century-ranch status of the Ford Ranch during route selection. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 144–145.
CULTURAL RESOURCES
Archaeological sites, cemeteries, and cultural-resource locations are properly considered under both the historical-values and environmental-integrity criteria.
The Commission may assign substantial weight to avoidance of known cultural resources.
The Commission may consider not only direct impacts to cultural resources but also proximity impacts resulting from construction, maintenance, access roads, pull sites, and associated facilities.
The existence of approximately 100 archaeological sites and 23 cemeteries within 1,000 feet of candidate routes supports careful consideration of cultural-resource impacts. Findings 31–40.
The record demonstrates that portions of Routes 392, 410 and 894/894 WM1 traverse areas of elevated archaeological sensitivity and have greater impact on cultural resources than Route 487. Findings 53, 56, 65, 73.
HUNTING, WILDLIFE MANAGEMENT, AND RECREATIONAL USES
Hunting operations and wildlife-management activities constitute legitimate components of community values.
The Commission may consider impacts to hunting practices resulting from vegetation clearing and creation of wide transmission rights-of-way.
The testimony regarding bow-hunting concealment and right-of-way clearing constitutes evidence of recreational and wildlife-management impacts. Findings 44–45.
The Commission may consider impacts on wildlife habitat management and hunting-related land uses when balancing routing factors.
EXISTING CORRIDOR UTILIZATION
The Commission has long recognized the value of utilizing existing compatible rights-of-way and consolidating infrastructure where feasible.
Utilization of existing transmission corridors reduces fragmentation of previously undisturbed lands.
Consolidation of transmission facilities into existing corridors is a legitimate routing objective.
The Commission may assign substantial weight to compatible right-of-way utilization and transmission-line paralleling.
Evidence that feasible existing-corridor alternatives were not fully evaluated may be considered when assessing the relative merits of competing routes. Findings 15, 48-51.
The Commission may consider evidence that Applicants did not evaluate routing along portions of existing northern or southern transmission corridors. Findings 48-51.
ROUTE 392
Route 392 may be rejected because it creates substantially greater residential impacts than Routes 410, 487 or 894/894 WM1. Finding 52.
Route 392 may be rejected because it creates substantially greater cultural-resource impacts than Routes 487 or 894/894 WM1. Finding 53.
The Commission is not required to select Route 392 merely because it performs favorably on certain corridor-utilization metrics.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 392 overemphasizes corridor utilization at the expense of residential, cultural-resource and other impacts.
ROUTE 410
Route 410 may be rejected because the record does not establish superior performance on the statutory routing criteria.
The record does not establish that Route 410 provides superior community-value, historical-value, environmental, or cultural-resource performance.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 410 does not provide a superior overall route balance when compared with Route 487. Findings 56-57.
ROUTE 487
The record supports a conclusion that Route 487 provides superior utilization of compatible rights-of-way. Findings 55, 59, 60 64, 66, 75, 76.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 487 provides superior utilization of existing transmission infrastructure over Routes 894/894 WM1. Findings 67, 76.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 487 appropriately balances cultural-resource impacts. Findings 31–32, 53, 56, 61, 65, 73.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 487 provides acceptable environmental and land-use performance. Findings 59-61.
The Commission may assign substantial weight to Staff's recommendation of Route 487. Finding 62.
Staff's conclusion that Route 487 possesses the greatest overall advantages constitutes substantial evidence supporting route selection. Poole Direct Testimony, at 65.
The evidence demonstrates that Route 487 is shorter than Routes 392, 410, 894 and 894 WM1, crosses fewer streams, and traverses less area identified as having high archaeological or historical-site potential.
ROUTE 894
The Commission may consider Route 894's lower habitable-structure count as a positive routing factor.
The Commission is not required to assign controlling weight to habitable-structure counts.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 utilizes substantially less compatible right-of-way than Route 487. Findings 59, 64, 72.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 is longer than Route 487. Finding 68.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 crosses more streams than Route 487.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 underperforms Route 487 on corridor utilization and infrastructure consolidation. Findings 59-60, 64, 66.
The Commission may reject Route 894 despite its lower habitable-structure count because the Commission must balance all routing criteria rather than a single metric.
ROUTE 894 Western Mod 1
The Commission may consider Route 894 WM1's lower habitable-structure count as a positive routing factor.
The Commission is not required to assign controlling weight to habitable-structure counts.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 WM1 utilizes substantially less compatible right-of-way than Route 487. Findings 59-60, 72, 75.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 WM1 utilizes substantially less existing transmission infrastructure than Route 487. Findings 76.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 WM1 is longer than Route 487. Finding 68.
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 WM1 crosses more streams than Route 487. 
The record supports a conclusion that Route 894 WM1 underperforms Route 487 on corridor utilization and infrastructure consolidation. Findings 59-60, 72, 75, 76.
The Commission may reject Route 894 WM1 despite its lower habitable-structure count because the Commission must balance all routing criteria rather than a single metric.
ULTIMATE CONCLUSIONS
The record supports rejection of Route 392.
The record supports rejection of Route 410.
The record supports rejection of Routes 894 and 894 WM1.
The record supports rejection of any Route using Links M12, N2 and N12 due to elevated cultural, archeological and historical sensitivity.
Based on the totality of the evidence, Route 487 provides the most reasonable balance of:
community values;
historical values;
environmental integrity;
cultural-resource protection;
compatible right-of-way utilization;
existing transmission-line paralleling;
infrastructure consolidation; and
moderation of impacts on affected landowners. Findings 78-83.
Route 487 best satisfies the routing criteria established by PURA §37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §25.101.
The Commission should reject Routes 392, 410, 894 and 894 WM1 and select Route 487 because Route 487 better satisfies the statutory objective of maximizing utilization of existing compatible rights-of-way while maintaining comparable performance on cultural-resource and environmental criteria.
The Commission may reasonably conclude that Route 487 provides a superior balance of corridor utilization, historic-landscape preservation, cultural-resource protection, and cumulative landowner impacts when compared with other routes.



PART III
PROPOSED ORDER / PFD
I. OVERVIEW
The principal issue in this proceeding is route selection.
The Commission has previously determined that additional transmission infrastructure is necessary to support ERCOT reliability and implementation of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. The remaining question is which route best satisfies the requirements of PURA §37.056(c)(4) and Commission Rule 25.101.
The evidence establishes that no route is superior on every metric. Accordingly, the Commission must balance competing routing factors and determine which route provides the most reasonable overall accommodation of:
community values;
historical values;
environmental integrity;
recreational impacts;
cost;
service considerations;
prudent utilization of existing infrastructure; and
moderation of impacts on affected landowners.
After review of the entire record, the undersigned concludes that Route 487 provides the most reasonable balance of these factors and should be selected.
II. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD
PURA §37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider:
Community values;
Recreational and park areas;
Historical values;
Aesthetic values;
Environmental integrity; and
Probable improvement of service and lowering of cost to consumers.
The Commission has repeatedly recognized that route selection is not a mathematical exercise. No single factor controls. Rather, the Commission must weigh all routing criteria and determine which route best satisfies the statutory standard under the particular facts presented.
The Commission is not required to select Applicants' preferred route, nor is it required to select the route with the fewest habitable structures, shortest length, or lowest cost. Instead, the Commission may select any route supported by substantial evidence.
III. THE RECORD ESTABLISHES THAT FEASIBLE ALTERNATIVES EXISTED
Applicants argue that Route 894 emerged from an extensive routing process and therefore warrants selection.
The record demonstrates, however, that feasible alternatives existed and that not all constructible route combinations received equivalent evaluation.
Russell Marusak acknowledged that Applicants did not evaluate routing along the northern or southern existing-transmission corridors discussed during Bradbury's cross-examination. Findings 48-50.
The significance of this testimony is not that the Commission must select the northern or southern corridors. Rather, it demonstrates that substantial opportunities for infrastructure consolidation existed beyond Route 894 and that Route 894 was not uniquely capable of satisfying the routing criteria.
Accordingly, the record does not support according special deference to Route 894 merely because it emerged from Applicants' routing process.
IV. COMMUNITY VALUES FAVOR ROUTE 487
The evidence demonstrates that community values play an unusually important role in this proceeding.
Concho, and McCulloch Counties are characterized by:
large working ranches;
wildlife-management properties;
hunting operations;
agricultural lands; and
rural residential uses.
The evidence further demonstrates that these counties are already energized and supported by the existing electric grid.
Thus, these counties bear substantial project impacts while receiving comparatively limited project-specific benefits.
The Commission has long recognized that community values encompass more than population density and residence counts. Community values include the manner in which affected communities use and experience the landscape.
The testimony regarding ranching, wildlife management, hunting, and agricultural operations therefore constitutes relevant evidence under PURA §37.056(c)(4).
The undersigned finds that Route 487 better balances these values because it achieves substantial infrastructure consolidation without producing the excessive residential impacts associated with Route 392.
V. HISTORICAL VALUES FAVOR ROUTE 487
The record demonstrates that historical resources within the study area include both recorded archaeological sites and historic ranching landscapes.
The Ford Ranch evidence illustrates that historical values extend beyond individual structures and demonstrate that Routes 894/894 WM1 creates greater cultural-resource impacts than Route 487.
A major 765-kV transmission corridor may alter the setting, viewshed, and landscape integrity of historic ranch properties even where no historic structure is physically removed.
The Commission may properly consider these impacts under the historical-values criterion.
The evidence also demonstrates that Routes 392 and 410 creates significantly greater cultural-resource impacts than Route 487.
The undersigned therefore concludes that Route 487 better accommodates historical values than Route 392 while avoiding the corridor-utilization deficiencies associated with Routes 894/894 WM1.

VI. CULTURAL RESOURCE EVIDENCE FAVORS ROUTE 487
The record identifies approximately 100 archaeological sites and 23 cemeteries within 1,000 feet of candidate routes. 
Known sites include:
41CC331;
41CC350;
41MK47;
41MK48; 
The cultural-resource record demonstrates that the study area contains substantial archaeological sensitivity along Links M12, N2, N12.
Route 487 crosses approximately two recorded cultural-resource sites.
Route 392 crosses approximately sixteen recorded cultural-resource sites.
Route 410 crosses approximately seventeen recorded cultural-resource sites.
The magnitude of this difference is significant.
While corridor utilization is important, the Commission cannot ignore the substantially greater cultural-resource impacts associated with Route 392.
Accordingly, Routes 392 and 410 should be rejected.
VII. HUNTING AND RECREATIONAL IMPACTS ARE LEGITIMATE COMMUNITY-VALUE CONSIDERATIONS
Applicants argue that transmission-line impacts on hunting operations are speculative.
The record demonstrates otherwise.
Marusak acknowledged that bow hunting depends upon concealment and testified that he would not expect a bow-hunting stand within a cleared transmission right-of-way.
The undersigned finds this testimony persuasive.
The evidence establishes that creation of a 200-foot-wide transmission corridor can affect hunting practices, wildlife-management activities, and recreational use of ranch properties.
These impacts are properly considered under the community-values criterion.
VIII. ROUTE 487 BEST SATISFIES THE COMMISSION'S CORRIDOR UTILIZATION POLICIES
The strongest objective evidence in the record concerns corridor utilization.
Staff witness Poole testified that Route 487:
utilizes compatible ROW for approximately 49.64 percent of its length;
ranks among the strongest-performing routes on that metric; and
parallels approximately 116,431 feet of existing transmission infrastructure.
By contrast, Route 894 and Route 894 WM1:
utilize approximately 43.92 and 38.7 percent compatible ROW, respectively;
parallel only approximately 29,870 feet and 51,745 feet of existing transmission infrastructure, respectively.
Thus:
Route 487 utilizes approximately 63,000 additional feet of compatible ROW vs. Route 894 and 86,000 additional feet of compatible ROW vs. 894 WM1; and
Route 487 utilizes over two times the amount of existing transmission-line paralleling.
The Commission has consistently favored infrastructure consolidation where feasible.
No competing route better satisfies that objective while maintaining acceptable performance on the remaining statutory criteria.
IX. ROUTES 894 and 894 WESTERN MOD 1 OVEREMPHASIZE A SINGLE METRIC
Applicants' principal argument for Routes 894/894 WM1 is that they affect fewer habitable structures.
The record confirms that Route 894 contains approximately 85 habitable structures, Route 894 WM1 contains 80 habitable structures, compared to approximately 96 for Route 487.
The Commission acknowledges that this is a small but meaningful advantage.
However, route selection cannot be based solely on habitable structures.
Poole testified that routes such as Routes 894/894 WM1 are:
longer;
more expensive; and
utilize less compatible ROW than Route 487.
JAH-12 likewise demonstrates that Routes 894/894 WM1 performs favorably on habitable structures while being outperformed on multiple other routing criteria.
The undersigned therefore concludes that Route 894 and Route 894 WM1 places disproportionate emphasis on residence avoidance at the expense of corridor utilization and infrastructure consolidation.
X. ROUTE 410 DOES NOT PROVIDE A SUPERIOR BALANCE
The record does not establish that Route 410 performs better than Route 487 on any combination of routing criteria sufficient to justify route selection.
Route 410 ranks below Route 487 in compatible ROW/property-boundary paralleling.
Route 410 utilizes Link N12 that is part of a significant established cultural-archeological corridor.
Nor does the record establish superior performance on community values, historical values, or environmental integrity.
Accordingly, Route 410 should be rejected.
XI. STAFF'S RECOMMENDATION IS ENTITLED TO SUBSTANTIAL WEIGHT
Staff witness John Poole conducted an independent review of the routing record.
Poole recommended Route 487.
Poole further concluded that Route 487 possesses the greatest overall advantages among the proposed alternatives.
Although the Commission is not bound by Staff's recommendation, the recommendation constitutes substantial evidence supporting Route 487.
The undersigned finds Staff's recommendation persuasive because it is consistent with the objective route-comparison data contained in the record.
XII. ULTIMATE DETERMINATION
The evidence establishes:
Route 392 creates excessive residential and cultural-resource impacts.
Route 410 does not provide superior overall performance.
Routes 894/894 WM1 underperform Route 487 in corridor utilization and infrastructure consolidation.
Route 487 provides strong corridor utilization, favorable environmental performance, acceptable cultural-resource impacts, and substantial infrastructure consolidation.
Most importantly, Route 487 achieves the best overall balance of the statutory routing criteria.
The undersigned therefore concludes that if a route is to be selected, Route 487 should be selected as the certificated route for the Bell County East Switch–Big Hill East 765-kV Transmission Line Project.

RECOMMENDATION
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED THAT:
Grant the Joint Application in part;
Route 392 is DENIED.
Route 410 is DENIED.
Applicants' preferred Route 894 is DENIED;
Route 894 Western Mod 1 is DENIED;
Route 487 is SELECTED as the approved route for the project.
Prior to construction, Applicants shall complete all required cultural-resource investigations and coordination with the Texas Historical Commission.
Applicants shall implement all mitigation measures required by the Commission's Environmental Assessment and Cultural Resources recommendations.
Applicants shall file revised route maps and centerline descriptions reflecting Route 487.
All relief not expressly granted herein is DENIED.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Mark Allan Bradbury

I, Mark Allan Bradbury ("Pro-Se Intervenor # 634") respectfully submit these
Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law regarding the routing of the
proposed 765 kV transmission line affecting Concho, and McCulloch Counties,
Texas on behalf of myself and Heart of Texas Bowhunting, LLC.



PARTI
PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT
I.   Jurisdiction and Need

     1. Applicants seek CCN authority to construct the Bell County East-Big Hill 765-kV
        transmission project.
     2. The proposed transmission line would traverse portions of Bell, Burnet,
        Lampasas, McCulloch, Menard, Concho, Schleicher, Sutton, Crockett, Reagan,
        Irion, Tom Green, and surrounding counties.
     3. The proposed facility consists of extra-high-voltage transmission infrastructure
        including lattice and/or monopole structures, conductors, access roads,
        construction staging areas, and associated facilities.
     4. The project would require a permanent transmission easement corridor generally
        ranging from approximately 200 to 350 feet in width.
   5. Construction would require substantial temporary disturbance beyond the
     permanent easement for access roads, structure assembly areas, conductor
     pulling sites, material Iaydown yards, and construction staging areas.

  6. Jared Gurley further confirmed that the Project's purpose is associated with the
     Permian Basin Reliability Plan. Hearing Vol. 3 at 146-147.

  7. Jared Gurley also acknowledged that Concho and McCulloch Counties are
     already energized and supported by the existing electric grid. Hearing Vol. 3 at
     146-147.
  8. Commission Staff witness John Poole testified that the project is intended to

PROPOSED ORDER / PFD
I. OVERVIEW
   The principal issue in this proceeding is route selection.

   The Commission has previously determined that additional transmission
   infrastructure is necessary to support ERCOT reliability and implementation of the
   Permian Basin Reliability Plan. The remaining question is which route best satisfies
   the requirements of PURA §37.056(c)(4) and Commission Rule 25.101.
   The evidence establishes that no route is superior on every metric. Accordingly, the
   Commission must balance competing routing factors and determine which route
   provides the most reasonable overall accommodation of:
   •     community values;
   •     historical values;
   •     environmental integrity;
   •     recreational impacts;
   •     cost;
   •     service considerations;
   •     prudent utilization of existing infrastructure; and
   •     moderation of impacts on affected landowners.
   After review of the entire record, the undersigned concludes that Route 487 provides
   the most reasonable balance of these factors and should be selected.
Il. APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD
       PURA §37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission to consider:

       1. Community values;
       2. Recreational and park areas;

       3. Historical values;

       4. Aesthetic values;

       5. Environmental integrity; and
    6. Probable improvement of service and lowering of cost to consumers.

   The Commission has repeatedly recognized that route selection is not a
   mathematical exercise. No single factor controls. Rather, the Commission must
   weigh all routing criteria and determine which route best satisfies the statutory
   standard under the particular facts presented.
   The Commission is not required to select Applicants' preferred route, nor is it
   required to select the route with the fewest habitable structures, shortest length, or
   lowest cost. Instead, the Commission may select any route supported by
   substantial evidence.
Ill. THE RECORD ESTABLISHES THAT FEASIBLE ALTERNATIVES EXISTED
   Applicants argue that Route 894 emerged from an extensive routing process and
   therefore warrants selection.
   The record demonstrates, however, that feasible alternatives existed and that not
   all constructible route combinations received equivalent evaluation.
   Russell Marusak acknowledged that Applicants did not evaluate routing along the
   northern or southern existing-transmission corridors discussed during Bradbury's
   cross-examination. Findings 48-50.

   The significance of this testimony is not that the Commission must select the
   northern or southern corridors. Rather, it demonstrates that substantial
   opportunities for infrastructure consolidation existed beyond Route 894 and that
   Route 894 was not uniquely capable of satisfying the routing criteria.

   Accordingly, the record does not support according special deference to Route 894
   merely because it emerged from Applicants' routing process.

IV. COMMUNITY VALUES FAVOR ROUTE 487
   The evidence demonstrates that community values play an unusually important role
   in this proceeding.
   Concho, and McCulloch Counties are characterized by:
   •   large working ranches;
   •   wildlife-management properties;
   •   hunting operations;
   •   agricultural lands; and
   •   rural residential uses.
   The evidence further demonstrates that these counties are already energized and
  supported by the existing electric grid.
  Thus, these counties bear substantial project impacts while receiving comparatively
  limited project-specific benefits.
  The Commission has long recognized that community values encompass more than
  population density and residence counts. Community values include the manner in
  which affected communities use and experience the landscape.
  The testimony regarding ranching, wildlife management, hunting, and agricultural
  operations therefore constitutes relevant evidence under PURA §37.056(c)(4).

  The undersigned finds that Route 487 better balances these values because it
  achieves substantial infrastructure consolidation without producing the excessive
  residential impacts associated with Route 392.

V. HISTORICAL VALUES FAVOR ROUTE 487
  The record demonstrates that historical resources within the study area include both
  recorded archaeological sites and historic ranching landscapes.
  The Ford Ranch evidence illustrates that historical values extend beyond individual
  structures and demonstrate that Routes 894/894 WM1 creates greater cultural-
  resource impacts than Route 487.

  A major 765-kV transmission corridor may alter the setting, viewshed, and
  landscape integrity of historic ranch properties even where no historic structure is
  physically removed.
  The Commission may properly consider these impacts under the historical-values
  criterion.
  The evidence also demonstrates that Routes 392 and 410 creates significantly
  greater cultural-resource impacts than Route 487.

  The undersigned therefore concludes that Route 487 better accommodates
  historical values than Route 392 while avoiding the corridor-utilization deficiencies
  associated with Routes 894/894 WM1.



VI. CULTURAL RESOURCE EVIDENCE FAVORS ROUTE 487
  The record identifies approximately 100 archaeological sites and 23 cemeteries
  within 1,000 feet of candidate routes.
  Known sites include:
   •   41 CC331;
  •   41 CC350;
  •   41 MK47;
  •   41 MK48;
  The cultural-resource record demonstrates that the study area contains substantial
  archaeological sensitivity along Links M12, N2, N12.

  Route 487 crosses approximately two recorded cultural-resource sites.

  Route 392 crosses approximately sixteen recorded cultural-resource sites.

  Route 410 crosses approximately seventeen recorded cultural-resource sites.

  The magnitude of this difference is significant.

  While corridor utilization is important, the Commission cannot ignore the
  substantially greater cultural-resource impacts associated with Route 392.

  Accordingly, Routes 392 and 410 should be rejected.

VII. HUNTING AND RECREATIONAL IMPACTS ARE LEGITIMATE COMMUNITY-
VALUE CONSIDERATIONS
  Applicants argue that transmission-line impacts on hunting operations are
  speculative.
  The record demonstrates otherwise.

  Marusak acknowledged that bow hunting depends upon concealment and testified
  that he would not expect a bow-hunting stand within a cleared transmission right-of-
  way.
  The undersigned finds this testimony persuasive.

  The evidence establishes that creation of a 200-foot-wide transmission corridor can
  affect hunting practices, wildlife-management activities, and recreational use of
  ranch properties.
  These impacts are properly considered under the community-values criterion.

Vlll. ROUTE 487 BEST SATISFIES THE COMMISSION'S CORRIDOR UTILIZATION
POLICIES
  The strongest objective evidence in the record concerns corridor utilization.

  Staff witness Poole testified that Route 487:
  •   utilizes compatible ROW for approximately 49.64 percent of its length;
   •   ranks among the strongest-performing routes on that metric; and
  •   parallels approximately 116,431 feet of existing transmission infrastructure.
  By contrast, Route 894 and Route 894 WM1:

  •   utilize approximately 43.92 and 38.7 percent compatible ROW, respectively;
  •   parallel only approximately 29,870 feet and 51,745 feet of existing transmission
      infrastructure, respectively.
  Thus:

  •   Route 487 utilizes approximately 63,000 additional feet of compatible ROW vs.
      Route 894 and 86,000 additional feet of compatible ROW vs. 894 WM1; and

  •   Route 487 utilizes over two times the amount of existing transmission-line
      paralleling.
      The Commission has consistently favored infrastructure consolidation where
      feasible.
      No competing route better satisfies that objective while maintaining acceptable
      performance on the remaining statutory criteria.
IX. ROUTES 894 and 894 WESTERN MOD 1 OVEREMPHASIZE A SINGLE METRIC
  Applicants' principal argument for Routes 894/894 WM1 is that they affect fewer
  habitable structures.
  The record confirms that Route 894 contains approximately 85 habitable structures,
  Route 894 WM1 contains 80 habitable structures, compared to approximately 96 for
  Route 487.

  The Commission acknowledges that this is a small but meaningful advantage.
  However, route selection cannot be based solely on habitable structures.

  Poole testified that routes such as Routes 894/894 WM1 are:
  •   longer;
  •   more expensive; and
  •   utilize less compatible ROW than Route 487.
  JAH-12 likewise demonstrates that Routes 894/894 WM1 performs favorably on
  habitable structures while being outperformed on multiple other routing criteria.
   The undersigned therefore concludes that Route 894 and Route 894 WM1 places
  disproportionate emphasis on residence avoidance at the expense of corridor
  utilization and infrastructure consolidation.
X. ROUTE 410 DOES NOT PROVIDE A SUPERIOR BALANCE
  The record does not establish that Route 410 performs better than Route 487 on any
  combination of routing criteria sufficient to justify route selection.
  Route 410 ranks below Route 487 in compatible ROW/property-boundary
  paralleling.
  Route 410 utilizes Link N12 that is part of a significant established cultural-
  archeological corridor.
  Nor does the record establish superior performance on community values, historical
  values, or environmental integrity.
  Accordingly, Route 410 should be rejected.

XI. STAFF'S RECOMMENDATION IS ENTITLED TO SUBSTANTIAL WEIGHT
  Staff witness John Poole conducted an independent review of the routing record.
  Poole recommended Route 487.

  Poole further concluded that Route 487 possesses the greatest overall advantages
  among the proposed alternatives.
  Although the Commission is not bound by Staffs recommendation, the
  recommendation constitutes substantial evidence supporting Route 487.

  The undersigned finds Staffs recommendation persuasive because it is consistent
  with the objective route-comparison data contained in the record.
XII. ULTIMATE DETERMINATION
  The evidence establishes:

  •   Route 392 creates excessive residential and cultural-resource impacts.

  •   Route 410 does not provide superior overall performance.

  •   Routes 894/894 WM1 underperform Route 487 in corridor utilization and
      infrastructure consolidation.
  •   Route 487 provides strong corridor utilization, favorable environmental
      performance, acceptable cultural-resource impacts, and substantial infrastructure
      consolidation.
 Most importantly, Route 487 achieves the best overall balance of the statutory
routing criteria.
The undersigned therefore concludes that if a route is to be selected, Route 487
should be selected as the certificated route for the Bell County East Switch-Big Hill
East 765-kV Transmission Line Project.
 RECOMMENDATION
  IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED THAT:
  1. Grant the Joint Application in part;
  2. Route 392 is DENIED.

  3. Route 410 is DENIED.

  4. Applicants' preferred Route 894 is DENIED;

  5. Route 894 Western Mod 1 is DENIED;

  6. Route 487 is SELECTED as the approved route for the project.

  7. Prior to construction, Applicants shall complete all required cultural-resource
     investigations and coordination with the Texas Historical Commission.
  8. Applicants shall implement all mitigation measures required by the Commission's
     Environmental Assessment and Cultural Resources recommendations.
  9. Applicants shall file revised route maps and centerline descriptions reflecting
     Route 487.

  10. All relief not expressly granted herein is DENIED.
